Tell me about the Rosetta mission and what it found at comet 67P.

The Rosetta mission was an Italian-European space mission launched by the European Space Agency (ESA) in 2004. Its primary goal was to study comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko. The mission successfully orbited the comet and deployed the Philae lander, which touched down on the comet's surface in November 2014. 

Rosetta provided valuable data on the comet's composition, structure, and environment. It discovered that the comet is composed of ice, dust, and rocky material, and its surface is covered with craters and valleys. The mission also revealed that the comet's tail extends for thousands of kilometers, and it is constantly being replenished by material from the solar wind. 

One of the most significant findings was the discovery of a complex network of ice and dust structures, which suggested that the comet had a history of activity and possibly even a past atmosphere. The mission also provided insights into the early solar system by studying the composition of the comet, which is considered a "primitive" body. The data from Rosetta have been instrumental in understanding the formation and evolution of the solar system.

67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko

67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko (abbreviated 67P or 67P/C–G and nicknamed "Chury") is a Jupiter-family comet. It is originally from the Kuiper belt and has an orbital period of 6.45 years as of 2012, a rotation period of approximately 12.4 hours, and a maximum velocity of 135,000 km/h (38 km/s; 84,000 mph). Churyumov–Gerasimenko is approximately 4.3 by 4.1 km (2.7 by 2.5 mi) at its longest and widest dimensions. It was first observed on photographic plates in 1969 by Soviet astronomers Klim Ivanovych Churyumov and Svetlana Ivanovna Gerasimenko, after whom it is named. It most recently came to perihelion (closest approach to the Sun) on 2 November 2021, and will next come to perihelion on 9 April 2028.
Churyumov–Gerasimenko was the destination of the European Space Agency's Rosetta mission, launched on 2 March 2004. Rosetta rendezvoused with Churyumov–Gerasimenko on 6 August 2014 and entered orbit on 10 September 2014. Rosetta's lander, Philae, landed on the comet's surface on 12 November 2014, becoming the first spacecraft to land on a comet nucleus. On 30 September 2016, the Rosetta spacecraft ended its mission by landing on the comet in its Maʽat region.

Rosetta (spacecraft)

Rosetta was a space probe built by the European Space Agency that launched on 2 March 2004. Along with Philae, its lander module, Rosetta performed a detailed study of comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko (67P). During its journey to the comet, the spacecraft performed flybys of Earth, Mars, and the asteroids 21 Lutetia and 2867 Šteins. It was launched as the third cornerstone mission of the ESA's Horizon 2000 programme, after SOHO / Cluster and XMM-Newton. The total cost of the mission was about €1.3 billion (US$1.8 billion).
On 6 August 2014, the spacecraft reached the comet and performed a series of manoeuvers to eventually orbit the comet at distances of 30 to 10 kilometres (19 to 6 mi). On 12 November, its lander module Philae performed the first successful landing on a comet, though its battery power ran out two days later. Communications with Philae were briefly restored in June and July 2015, but due to diminishing solar power, Rosetta's communications module with the lander was turned off on 27 July 2016. On 30 September 2016, the Rosetta spacecraft ended its mission by hard-landing on the comet in its Ma'at region.
